st-mark-the-evangelist.imageCredit: Sixteenth-century Gospel illumination of Mark; public domain via Wikimedia Commons
sections: A name in the early Church

The New Testament refers to John called Mark in Acts. A house associated with his mother Mary is a gathering place for believers in Jerusalem. Later passages place a Mark among the companions of Barnabas, Paul and Peter. The precise relationship among all references is discussed by historians, but the Church’s tradition sees in him an important witness of the apostolic generation. His story is less a continuous biography than a collection of glimpses into communities learning to carry the Gospel beyond Jerusalem.
Travel and a difficult parting

Acts recounts Mark accompanying Barnabas and Paul on a journey and then leaving them. When Barnabas wants to take him on a later journey, Paul disagrees. The two missionaries go separate ways. The text does not tell us everything Mark felt or why he departed. It does show that relationships among saints were not free of sharp disagreement. Other New Testament references speak positively of Mark’s usefulness in ministry, reminding readers that one difficult episode need not define a whole life.
Peter and an ancient tradition

First Peter sends greetings from Mark, describing him with affectionate language. Early Christian testimony associated Mark with Peter’s preaching and with the Gospel that bears Mark’s name. The history of how the text took its final form is studied and debated. A Catholic reading can honor this early testimony while being honest that the New Testament does not supply a signed manuscript or a complete account of the book’s composition. Mark’s Gospel itself is the principal text for understanding its witness to Jesus.
The Gospel’s pace

Mark begins with John the Baptist and Jesus’ public ministry, moving quickly into healings, conflict, teaching and the way to Jerusalem. It does not include an infancy narrative. Readers repeatedly see disciples who struggle to understand Jesus and a Lord who continues to teach them. At the center stands the question of who Jesus is and what it means to follow him along the path of the Cross. The Gospel’s speed invites a reader to keep going until the Passion and Resurrection rather than stop at a favorite miracle.
A word to a suffering community

Mark gives substantial space to the last days of Jesus. Fear, misunderstanding, abandonment and fidelity all appear there. Its account has spoken powerfully to Christians under pressure, though a precise occasion and audience for its composition remain debated. The Gospel does not ask readers to pretend that discipleship eliminates fear. It asks them to look again at Jesus, whose suffering and Resurrection change the meaning of faithful witness. This is one reason the book remains more than an early historical source: it is read aloud in the Church’s worship.
Later memories and their limits

Tradition associates Mark with Alexandria and with the church there, while Venice later became a famous center of devotion to him. The New Testament does not narrate his ministry in Alexandria or describe his death. These later histories should be identified as traditions. The winged lion often pictured beside him comes from Christian symbolism for the four evangelists, not from an episode of his life. Art and local memory can help people approach the saint when they are not confused with the biblical record.
Feast and reading

Mark’s feast is 25 April. The Church remembers an evangelist whose short Gospel has formed prayer and preaching for centuries. A useful way to celebrate is to read the book in several sittings, noting how Jesus calls, heals, questions and walks toward Jerusalem. Mark’s own story also invites patience with imperfect co-workers: a painful separation need not prevent later service. What lasts most clearly is the witness to Christ that Christians have received under his name.
A companion whose story continues

Mark’s departure during an early journey led to a real argument between Barnabas and Paul. Acts does not report a neat conversation in which every feeling is resolved. Later references to a Mark in apostolic circles show that Christian service continued. The sequence allows room for failure, disagreement, changed judgments and renewed usefulness. A community should not turn one conflict into a person’s permanent identity. The difficult passage can also encourage fair treatment of companions whose reasons for a decision are not fully known.
Reading Mark aloud

Mark’s Gospel was written for hearing as well as private reading. Its repeated movements from one place or encounter to another bring listeners into the urgency of Jesus’ ministry. A person who reads it aloud can hear how questions accumulate: who is this man, why do the disciples misunderstand, and what does the Cross reveal? The book’s brevity helps a group read it from beginning to end, allowing its Passion account to illuminate earlier scenes.
The women at the tomb

Mark’s account of the women visiting the tomb ends, in its earliest recoverable form, with fear and an announcement that Jesus has been raised. Manuscripts also preserve longer endings, which deserve careful attention in Bible editions. The textual history is an opportunity to learn how the Church received ancient writings, not a reason to hide the Resurrection witness. The women come to care for Jesus’ body and are sent toward news greater than their expectation.
A saint behind the symbol

The winged lion has made Mark recognizable in churches and manuscripts. In Venice it appears in civic art as well. A symbol can travel widely and gather new associations, but a life story still needs the early texts: a named companion, relationships with apostolic leaders and a Gospel focused on Jesus. Seeing both the symbol and the text helps a visitor move from an impressive picture toward a deeper reading of the saint’s witness.

st-luke-the-evangelist.famousFor: The Gospel according to Luke and Acts of the Apostles, with special attention to mercy and the early Church
st-luke-the-evangelist.imageCredit: Eighteenth-century icon of Luke the Evangelist; public domain via Wikimedia Commons
sections: A companion remembered

The New Testament names Luke among Paul’s companions, and Colossians calls a Luke a beloved physician. Church tradition connects this person with the author of the Gospel according to Luke and Acts. The exact details of his birthplace, training and later movements are less certain than devotional accounts sometimes imply. Keeping those limits visible lets a reader appreciate what is clear: the Church has received two major writings associated with Luke and remembers a companion in the work of spreading the faith.
A two-part work

Luke’s Gospel opens with a prologue explaining the author’s care in passing on an orderly account. Acts continues the story after Jesus’ Resurrection and Ascension, following the Spirit’s work in the early communities. Together the books travel from the announcement of Jesus’ birth toward the witness of the Church in Rome. They were composed with theological purpose and should be read as works of the ancient world rather than modern transcripts. Their narrative joins people and events to the larger question of how salvation reaches beyond one place.
Mary and the beginnings

Luke gives considerable space to Mary, Elizabeth, Zechariah, Simeon and Anna. Their responses to God form a chorus at the beginning of the Gospel. The annunciation and visitation have nourished the Church’s prayer, including the words of the Hail Mary and the Magnificat. Luke presents women and men who wait, question, praise and respond. This attention makes the beginning of the Gospel more than background to Jesus’ adult life; it shows the good news arriving among particular families and communities.
Stories of mercy

The Good Samaritan, the lost sheep and the father who welcomes a lost son are among the stories Luke preserves. They call readers to see a neighbor where convention might have taught them to pass by. Luke also gives voice to people who are poor, sick or excluded and records Jesus’ concern for them. His emphasis on mercy does not mean that change is unnecessary. The invitation to return to God comes with a call to justice and generosity.
The road after Easter

In Luke 24, two disciples travel toward Emmaus in disappointment. The risen Jesus joins them, opens the Scriptures and is recognized in the breaking of bread. Their journey from sorrow to witness is part of Luke’s way of showing how faith grows through word and shared life. Acts then opens with the Spirit’s gift at Pentecost and follows the first communities. Readers can see connections between what Jesus did and what his followers, strengthened by the Spirit, begin to do.
Paul and the reach of the Gospel

The later chapters of Acts recount Paul’s travels, arrests and journey to Rome. Pope Francis has reflected on the sea voyage and shipwreck as a setting in which the Gospel continues its journey even through apparent setbacks. The account ends without describing Paul’s death, leaving readers with a living story of proclamation. That ending should not be filled with invented certainty about Luke’s own final days. His witness draws attention to the Word continuing beyond the limits of the book.
A feast for attentive readers

Luke’s feast falls on 18 October. His traditional association with medicine and art reflects both the reference to a physician and the rich portrayal of people in his Gospel; accounts of him painting Mary belong to later tradition. One can honor his memory by reading Luke and Acts together, noticing whom Jesus welcomes and how the Church learns to share resources. The writer invites careful attention to individual lives within the larger movement of God’s mercy.
Voices in the infancy story

Luke allows Elizabeth, Mary, Zechariah and Simeon to respond to the news of God’s work in distinct ways. Their songs and prayers are still used in Christian worship. A reader who knows the story only from a Christmas image may miss its attention to people who have waited, feared, questioned and hoped for years. The Gospel begins with individual voices before it widens to the ministry of Jesus and the journey of the Church.
The table and the road

Luke records many meals and journeys. Jesus shares tables with different people and teaches disciples while traveling toward Jerusalem. After Easter, he meets two followers on a road. These repeated settings keep faith connected to conversation, hospitality and the movement of ordinary lives. They can also sharpen a moral question: who is welcome at a table, and who is left outside? Luke’s stories of mercy ask for more than admiration of a generous character.
A physician in the tradition

Colossians refers to a Luke as a beloved physician, giving rise to his patronage of medical workers. The text does not provide a description of a medical practice or a list of patients. The tradition nevertheless draws attention to Luke’s careful interest in human suffering and healing as portrayed in the Gospel. A health worker remembering his feast might pray for skill and compassion together, while a patient might find comfort in the Gospel’s attention to people whom others overlook.
A writer attentive to women

Luke’s Gospel and Acts name women who pray, listen, give material support and speak to others about faith. Mary’s role is distinctive, but it is not the only one. The women at Jesus’ tomb bring news to the apostles; later communities include women who offer hospitality and service. Reading the two books together helps prevent these witnesses from becoming isolated decorative figures. They belong to the movement of the Gospel across families, cities and cultures.
